newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan riot police block road to gunman's village.
newsitem.headline: Jordan riot police block road to gunman's village.

text.p: Jordanian riot police set up a roadblock on Monday to prevent sympathisers of the Jordanian soldier who gunned down seven Israeli schoolgirls last week from paying respects to his family.

More than 50 security forces and special police clutching batons and shields stopped a procession of cars carrying dozens of sympathisers at the northern village of Muzeireeb about five kilometres (three miles) outside Ibdr, home of gunman Ahmed Mousa al-Daqamsa.

"We have instruction to prevent you from entering the town," regional police commander Abdul Salam al-Jaafra told a delegation of Islamist deputies, opposition figure and lawyers, who had gathered on the road to Ibdr.
Jordan's King Hussein consoled families of the dead school girls in Israel on Sunday, saying Jordanians were deeply shamed by the shooting.
But the delegates disputed the official Jordanian view that the shooting was the isolated act of an insane criminal, and local villagers said Daqamsa was regarded by many as a hero.

"This youth has inside him a buried burning rage against the Israeli occupier, and I think this could have motivated his attack," said Samih Khreis, a lawyer who said he was campaigning to ensure that Daqamsa received a fair trial.

"The authorities are taking their orders from Israel, while the Jordanian people are with this soldier and consider him a hero," said Faris Zaher al-Fayez from Bani Sakhr tribe, who was also trying to visit Daqamsa.
Villagers said Daqamsa was becoming a cult figure in northern highland areas and the cluster of small villages, including Ibdr, about 100 km (60 miles) north of Amman.
The region, overlooking Israel, is inhabited by bedouin tribes from the East Bank, regarded as a bedrock of King Hussein's support.
They repeated stories circulating that Daqamsa only took his rifle and began shooting wildly after the Israeli teenagers provoked him while he was performing early noon prayers.

They said Ibdr was one of the villages which bore the brunt of Israeli shelling in reprisal for Palestinian guerrilla attacks from the Jordan Valley in 1969, and family stories of the bombardment of his village could explain his behaviour.
Officials say Daqamsa was born two years later, in 1971.
The group said they had already collected around 1,500 dinars ($2,000) to help support Daqamsa's family.
The shooting took place in northern Baqoura area, part of Jordan which was leased to Israel in the 1994 peace treaty but which Jordanians need a special security pass to enter.
Many Jordanians are infuriated at the lease deal they believe perpetuates the presence of a former enemy on their territory.

"This act is not an individual act but within the context of a long string of Israeli crimes that provoked the nation and pushed the soldier to act the way he did," said Hamam Said, a leading parliamentary deputy of the Islamic Action Front.
